details:
**Easter Rising**
A 1916 armed rebellion in Dublin against British rule, launched on Easter Monday when rebels seized the General Post Office and Patrick Pearse read the Proclamation of the Irish Republic. The British crushed it within a week and executed sixteen leaders, including Pearse and James Connolly, which turned public opinion toward independence. Éamon de Valera, who commanded at Boland's Mill, was spared partly because he was born in America.

**Great Famine (Potato Famine)**
The famine of 1845-1852, caused by the potato blight Phytophthora infestans, in which about a million people died and millions emigrated on overcrowded "coffin ships," with 1847 remembered as "Black '47." Robert Peel repealed the Corn Laws in response, but Lord John Russell's government and official Charles Trevelyan held to laissez-faire policies; the "Gregory Clause" denied relief to anyone holding over a quarter acre, and people who converted to Protestantism for food were called "soupers."

**Michael Collins and Éamon de Valera**
The two leading figures of Irish independence. Collins ran the IRA's intelligence war and signed the 1921 Anglo-Irish Treaty, while de Valera opposed the treaty, and their sides fought the Irish Civil War of 1922-1923, in which Collins was killed. De Valera later founded Fianna Fáil and became Taoiseach and president.

**Charles Stewart Parnell**
The 19th-century leader of the Irish Home Rule movement and president of the Land League. Forged letters by journalist Richard Pigott falsely tied him to the Phoenix Park Murders, and he is remembered each year on Ivy Day, the anniversary of his death.

**Sinn Féin, Fianna Fáil, and Fine Gael**
Sinn Féin is the nationalist party founded by Arthur Griffith. Ireland's two main modern parties came out of its treaty split: Fianna Fáil, founded by the anti-treaty de Valera, and Fine Gael, from the pro-treaty side. The head of government is called the Taoiseach, and the parliament is the Dáil.

**Black and Tans**
British auxiliary police, mostly World War I veterans and named for their mixed uniforms, sent to Ireland during the 1919-1921 War of Independence against the IRA. They became notorious for reprisals against civilians, and many Anglo-Irish "Big Houses" were burned during that war.

**Home Rule**
The movement for a self-governing Irish parliament within the United Kingdom, started by Isaac Butt and led by Parnell. Prime Minister William Gladstone backed Home Rule bills in 1886 and 1893, but both failed.

**Phoenix Park Murders**
The 1882 stabbing of Chief Secretary for Ireland Lord Frederick Cavendish and Under-Secretary Thomas Burke in Dublin's Phoenix Park by the Invincibles, a radical nationalist group. Parnell was falsely accused of approving of the killings.

**Land League and the "Three Fs"**
The Irish National Land League, founded by Michael Davitt in 1879, led the "Land War" for tenant farmers' rights. Its goals were the "Three Fs": fair rent, fixity of tenure, and free sale.

**Roger Casement**
An Irish nationalist and former British diplomat who tried to bring German rifles to the Easter Rising on a ship disguised as the Norwegian SS Aud. He was executed for treason; he was said to be "hanged on a comma" because the conviction depended on how a comma in an old treason law was read, and the "Black Diaries" were used to discredit him.

**Bloody Sunday (1920) and the Cairo Gang**
On November 21, 1920, Michael Collins's assassination unit, "the Squad" or "Twelve Apostles," killed British intelligence agents known as the "Cairo Gang." Later that day, British forces opened fire on a crowd at a Gaelic football match at Croke Park. Collins had earlier organized protests while held at the Frongoch internment camp after the Easter Rising.

**The Troubles and the Good Friday Agreement**
The roughly thirty-year conflict in Northern Ireland between mostly Catholic nationalists, including the Provisional IRA, and mostly Protestant unionists such as Ian Paisley's Democratic Unionist Party, which was ended by the 1998 Good Friday Agreement. IRA attacks included the 1984 Brighton hotel bombing, which nearly killed Margaret Thatcher.

**Bobby Sands and the Maze hunger strike**
The "blanket" and "dirty" protests by IRA prisoners at the Maze Prison against the loss of Special Category (political prisoner) status grew into the 1981 hunger strike led by Bobby Sands. Sands was elected to the British Parliament during the strike and died weeks later.

**Bloody Sunday (1972)**
A massacre in the Bogside area of Derry, Northern Ireland, in which soldiers of the British Parachute Regiment shot 26 unarmed civil-rights marchers, killing 14. It boosted support for the Provisional IRA, and the later Saville Inquiry found the killings unjustified.

**Cromwellian conquest and the plantations**
Oliver Cromwell's brutal 1649 conquest of Ireland, after which rebel land was seized under the Adventurers' Act and given to New Model Army veterans. Together with earlier English plantations in Munster and Ulster and the later anti-Catholic Penal Laws, it built the dominance of the Protestant Ascendancy.
